sources.citation: de Créqui-Montfort, Georges & Rivet, Paul. 1913. Linguistique bolivienne: La langue Saraveka. Journal de la Société des Américanistes 10: 497-540. DOI 10.3406/jsa.1913.2869.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: held in print at Harvard (Widener Library, call number 1271.09); ask your own library for a scan or interlibrary loan
sources.note: Nothing. States the Saraveka documents reduce to d'Orbigny's 23-word published list, a very short Weddell text (in Castelnau) and d'Orbigny's unpublished vocabulary which they print in full; body is lexical comparison with Arawak/Chiquito/Otuké plus grammatical notes (gender, number, prefixes nu-/no-, i-/e-, suffixes). No remark on accent, stress or prosody; a full-text search for stress/accent the article range for accent/tonique/prononc/syllabe finds only a note on a d'Orbigny transcription error (nol -> nuhe).

sources.citation: Ramirez, Henri & França, Maria Cristina Victorino de. 2019. Línguas Arawak da Bolívia. LIAMES 19: e019012, 1-71. DOI 10.20396/liames.v19i0.8655045.
sources.note: Has accent statements for Mojeño (Ignaciano) and Baure/Pauna, but Saraveka is only mentioned historically (pp. 50-51) as 'o sarave, um codialeto do pareci', a Paresi group that fled into the Chiquitos missions c. 1720-1730; no Saraveka data or prosodic remark.

sources.citation: d'Orbigny, Alcide. 1839. L'Homme américain (de l'Amérique méridionale), considéré sous ses rapports physiologiques et moraux. Tome 2. Paris: Pitois-Levrault. 'Nation Saravéca' pp. 171-174 (language remarks pp. 172-173); general remarks on the languages of Chiquitos province pp. 154-156.
sources.note: Nothing on accent. The only first-hand observer gives segmental impressions only: strong 'gutturation' of Spanish j in many words, 'la seule intonation dure ou peu euphonique; car elle n'a ni diphthongues, ni son nasal', has Spanish ch and French ch and z, frequent final i (Ejarati 'côtes') and Spanish u (Acunéchu 'femme'); body-part nouns begin with N-. Footnote: in 1831 only one old man still spoke it 'purement'.

sources.note: Only modern treatment of the Saraveka corpus (15 pp.); Ramirez re-transcribes historical wordlists (d'Orbigny, possibly Natterer's unpublished Saraveka list) and in comparable entries remarks on where the sources' accent marks fall; if any accent inference for Saraveka exists in print it is here.
